Why do a lot of things sound better when reverb is applied to them? (Whistling etc.)

Short answer:

It softens the sound waves and become more pleasing for your ear.

Long answer:

It could be argued that one of the core functions of our brain is to convolute our experiences and group them according to similarities in a high dimensional space. When you then experience something new, our brain finds where in this high-dimensional library the new experience fits, and you recognize it. Hence you can recognize for example a basket ball not only by its shape, but also its color, its sound, its conceptual relations, etc. Some pathways in certain dimensions are stronger (more used) than others, and therefore they are stronger indicators of what it is you are perceiving.

Now, the problem with such a model is that a strong and direct input disturbs or throws off the system (as seen in mathematical models), and gives the input a disproportionate significance. Therefore we have regulatory systems (in a simplified understanding of the brain largely located in the interplay between the Amygdala and Insula) that softens or convolutes the input before it goes further up in the higher brain functions. A shock is an example of this, where a sudden, disproportionate input (i.e. expecting there to be an extra step in the staircase) throws off the system and forces you to asses the situation and rethink the event until you've "softened" it to the point where it can be understood and you find the location in your library where it fits. With extreme events, your brain aren't able to categorize it properly and hence a trauma is born. When you later encounter a situation that touches upon the traumatic event (in any of the dimensions), you brain re-encounter this spot in the library that aren't properly ordered, and doesn't know what to do (to varying degrees depending on the trauma).

Hence we like soft things, yet sharp enough to create new experiences. Any sharp thing in any type of dimension (a sharp object (knife), a sharp sound (square wave), a sharp conceptual idea (ISIS), etc.), is uncomfortable, but less so if expected or understood.

So if we follow up on this theory, there are two reasons things sound better when reverb is applied to them:

  1. The sharp sounds are softened when the sound wave interferes with itself, hence being convoluted naturally before reaching the ear.
  2. We are given more dimensions to understand the sound through since reverberation adds complexity to the sound (more information), enabling us to relate it to a greater number of experiences.

Is taken off the top of my head and should be taken with a grain of philosophical and mathematical salt, but I feel it kind of makes sense.
